items.stem: Briefly explain why AB = b − a, where a and b are the position vectors of A and B.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the scalar product of perpendicular vectors is zero.
items.answer: v · w = |v||w| cos θ and cos 90° = 0, so the product is 0 regardless of the magnitudes.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: v · w = |v||w| cos θ and cos 90° = 0, so the product is 0 regardless of the magnitudes. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why v × w = −(w × v).
items.answer: Swapping the order reverses the direction given by the right-hand rule while keeping the magnitude |v||w| sin θ.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Swapping the order reverses the direction given by the right-hand rule while keeping the magnitude |v||w| sin θ. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "The scalar product of two vectors is a vector." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It is a scalar (a number); the vector product v × w is a vector.

items.stem: "The magnitude of 3i − 4j is 3 − 4 = −1." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Magnitude is √(3² + (−4)²) = 5; it is never negative.

items.stem: Explain why two lines in 3D can be neither parallel nor intersecting, unlike in 2D.
items.answer: In 3D lines can lie in different planes (e.g. one above the other at different heights), so they may never meet even though their directions differ; in 2D non-parallel lines always meet.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: In 3D lines can lie in different planes (e.g. one above the other at different heights), so they may never meet even though their directions differ; in 2D non-parallel lines always meet.
